prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "PROGRESSIVE CORP/OH/" (ticker PGR), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PGR", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Progressive Corporation
result.industry: Property and casualty insurance (mainly US personal auto)
markets: US private passenger auto insurance (direct and through independent agents)
US homeowners and renters insurance (Progressive Home)
US commercial auto insurance for small businesses and trucking
Insurance agency services (selling other carriers' policies)

mission.statement: We exist to help people move forward and live fully.
mission.plain: Progressive wants to protect people's cars, homes and businesses so a bad day doesn't stop them getting on with their lives.

about.plain: Progressive sells insurance, mostly for cars. People pay it a monthly or yearly fee, and if they crash or their car is damaged, Progressive pays to fix it or covers the costs. It also insures homes, motorcycles, boats and work trucks. It invests the money it holds until claims come in and earns interest on it.
about.customers: Ordinary drivers and homeowners across the US, plus small businesses and truckers, buying online, by phone or through local insurance agents.
about.everyday: It is the company behind the cheerful TV saleswoman Flo and the Snapshot app that rewards careful driving with lower prices.

money.plain: car, bike, boat and home insurance for families
insurance for work vans, trucks and small-business vehicles
interest and gains on the bonds and stocks it holds
commissions for selling other insurers' policies

result.summary: Yes. Progressive has a durable cost and data advantage in US auto insurance: decades of pricing know-how (usage-based Snapshot, very fine rating segments), the largest direct-to-consumer engine plus 40,000+ independent agencies, and the scale to outspend rivals on advertising. It became the No. 2 US auto insurer with an 18.60% share in 2025, almost level with State Farm (18.64%), while keeping its combined ratio at 87.4% in 2025. The advantage is in execution rather than any barrier customers can't cross, since auto insurance is a commodity that people can switch every six months.

pricingPower.evidence: Progressive's pricing power comes from pricing more accurately than rivals rather than charging more: it grew total policies in force 6% to 40.5M at Sept 30, 2026 while net premiums written rose only 4% in Q3 2026, meaning average premiums fell as it cut rates to win share; in a commodity market regulators must approve rate changes, and Florida forced about $1B of 2025 policyholder credits (2025 policyholder credit expense $1,224M) when profits ran too high.

moats.evidence: Flo, Jamie and the 'Name Your Price' tool make Progressive one of the best-known insurance brands in America, backed by one of the largest ad budgets in the industry; but brand lowers the cost of winning a customer rather than letting it charge more.
Auto policies renew every six or twelve months and comparison sites make shopping easy; bundling auto with Progressive Home and other lines raises retention somewhat.
More policies give more claims and telematics data, which sharpens pricing, but that is a scale/data effect rather than a true network effect between users.

With $81.7B of net premiums earned in 2025, Progressive spreads advertising, technology and claims infrastructure over a huge base, and its 2025 combined ratio of 87.4% left room to cut prices while staying very profitable.
The US auto insurance market is large and contested by dozens of national and regional carriers, so there is no natural limit on competitors.
Progressive sells both directly and through independent agents, while captive-agent rivals such as State Farm and Allstate find it hard to cut out their own agents to match a low-cost direct model.

Decades of granular rating segmentation, usage-based insurance (Snapshot), rapid rate-filing discipline and a culture that targets a 96 combined ratio while growing as fast as possible are hard to copy, as GEICO's and Allstate's 2022-2023 losses showed.
Its driving and claims dataset is large and proprietary, but rivals have their own data and no exclusive licence or asset protects Progressive.

customers.evidence: Customers keep coming: total policies in force rose 6% year on year to 40.5M at Sept 30, 2026, and Progressive ranked highest for service in J.D. Power's 2024 U.S. Insurance Digital Experience Study (score 737); like most auto insurers it still loses many customers each year to price shopping.

talent.evidence: Progressive ranked No. 19 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For 2026 (highest-ranked insurer, ninth year in a row) and No. 1 on Forbes' America's Best Employers for Company Culture 2026, with about 70,000 employees.

product.evidence: Its online quoting, Snapshot usage-based pricing, comparison-rate tool and app rank among the best in the industry (top service score in J.D. Power's 2024 Digital Experience Study), and it is the leading writer of commercial auto, though claims-satisfaction scores are not consistently best in class.

threats: Soft-market price war: after record margins (87.4% combined ratio in 2025) rivals such as GEICO and Allstate are cutting rates and spending more on advertising, and Progressive's Q3 2026 premiums grew only 4%
Rising claim costs from tariffs on cars and parts, medical inflation, and litigation ('social inflation') that can outrun approved rate increases
Regulation of profits and rates, such as Florida's excess-profit rule that led to about $1B of policyholder credits in 2025
Catastrophe and climate losses in the property (home) book, especially in Florida and Texas
Autonomous driving and advanced driver-assistance systems shrinking accident frequency and shifting liability from drivers to carmakers over the long run
Carmakers (e.g. Tesla Insurance) and tech platforms embedding insurance at the point of sale with their own vehicle data

ceo.name: Tricia Griffith
ceo.background: Joined Progressive in 1988 as a claims representative; former chief human resources officer, claims group president and COO of Personal Lines; Illinois State University graduate, Wharton advanced management program

c1.evidence: US auto insurance is a huge but mature market dating back a century, so Progressive leads (No. 2 at 18.60% share in 2025, near-tied with State Farm) an established rather than emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Progressive for lower prices built on better risk segmentation, Snapshot telematics and easy online quoting, and that pricing know-how and scale have kept it gaining share from 13.3% (2020) to 18.60% (2025).

c3.evidence: Most Americans know Progressive and its Flo ads, and it is the top direct-and-agency auto writer, but State Farm still holds a fractionally larger share (18.64%) and insurers are rarely recommended with enthusiasm.

c4.evidence: Its purpose, 'We exist to help people move forward and live fully', and its core values (Integrity, Golden Rule, Objectives, Excellence, Profit) are emphasised, but management is openly driven by a profit target (96 combined ratio) as much as by purpose.

c6.evidence: “Flo, cheap car insurance, Name Your Price, Snapshot” – the impression is mostly positive and friendly thanks to its ads, tempered by the general distrust people feel toward insurers' claims handling.

c7.evidence: The US private auto insurance market is very large (Progressive alone earned $81.7B of premiums in 2025) and grows with car repair inflation, but it rides no secular growth trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: Progressive is expanding in homeowners (Progressive Home) and commercial lines, but its vision of being the '#1 destination for insurance and other financial needs' remains largely within US property and casualty insurance.

m1.evidence: Tricia Griffith has a clear strategy (grow auto share, build home insurance to bundle, keep a 96 combined ratio) but is an operator rather than a visionary reshaping the future.

m2.evidence: Griffith is a 38-year company veteran who started as a claims representative in 1988 and manages for the long term, but she is not a founder.

m4.evidence: Griffith came up through claims and HR, launched Progressive's first diversity and inclusion program in 2007, and the company ranked No. 1 on Forbes' America's Best Employers for Company Culture 2026.

m5.evidence: Under Griffith the culture rated highly (Fortune 100 Best Companies No. 19 in 2026), but innovation such as Snapshot and online quoting largely predates her tenure.

m6.evidence: Griffith is deeply hands-on with operations and claims, but has no engineering background.

m7.evidence: Griffith is widely respected (Fortune Businessperson of the Year 2018) and emphasises employees and the Golden Rule, but there is no sign of a mission beyond running an excellent insurer.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Tricia Griffith giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Griffith is a low-key, respected operator rather than a famous outsized personality.

m9.evidence: Since she became CEO in 2016, revenue grew from $23.4B (2016) to $87.7B (2025) and diluted EPS from $1.76 to $19.23.

m10.evidence: Progressive is known for disciplined expense ratios and cost control, but it is also one of the biggest advertising spenders in US insurance, not a byword for frugality.

c10.evidence: It protects about 40.5 million US policies (Sept 2026) and pays claims that get people back on the road, but it serves only the US and solves a financial need rather than transforming lives.

p2.evidence: Pricing auto risk profitably at Progressive's scale is hard, as GEICO's and Allstate's 2022-2023 losses showed, but insurance is a well-understood product with many capable rivals.

f2.evidence: Insurers report no gross margin, and the pretax margin was 16.8% in 2020, fell to 1.9% in 2022 and recovered to 16.2% in 2025, so it has not risen over five years.

f3.evidence: Debt of $8.4B (June 2026) against $34.3B of equity, $97.2B of investments and $17.5B of 2025 operating cash flow; interest expense was only $278M in 2025.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $6.91B (2020) to $17.55B (2025) and pretax income from $7.17B to $14.22B, but both dipped in 2022 (cash flow $6.85B, pretax $0.92B).

v1.evidence: Progressive is often the cheapest quote for many drivers thanks to finer pricing and its comparison tool, but State Farm, GEICO and others win on price or service for many others, so it is not clearly best for everyone.

v2.evidence: No. 19 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For 2026 (highest-ranked insurer, nine years running) and No. 1 on Forbes' America's Best Employers for Company Culture 2026.

c5.evidence: Its insurance lets 40 million policyholders recover from crashes and storms, but if it disappeared, State Farm, GEICO, Allstate and others would absorb its customers, so drivers would mostly miss its prices and tools rather than an irreplaceable product.
